fields.definition: A spectral-processing technique that captures the frequency-domain content of a single analysis frame from an FFT/phase-vocoder analysis of a sound and repeats it during resynthesis, sustaining that one timbral moment for any length while its magnitude and phase spectrum stay fixed, producing a static drone or pad.
fields.plain_english: It grabs one tiny slice of a sound and holds it in place. The tone stays the same, but time seems to stop. A short note can turn into a long, steady hum.
fields.purpose_function: It extends a short or decaying sound into a continuous sustained texture; it exists so producers and sound designers can build drones, pads and ambiences from material that would otherwise fade away quickly.
fields.practical_application: A technician sets a freeze point on a held vowel, synth chord or cymbal wash in a spectral plugin or editor and captures it to make an evolving background pad or to sustain a tail under a transition.
common_mistakes: Freezing on a noisy transient, which gives a harsh or metallic drone instead of a smooth tone
Expecting a freeze to keep evolving on its own — the held spectrum is static unless you modulate it
Confusing a spectral freeze with looping a slice of audio; a freeze holds a reconstructed spectrum, not a repeated time segment
scenario_contexts: Turning a sustained vocal note into an ambient pad in a DAW
Holding a reverb tail or cymbal wash under a scene change in film sound design
Creating a tension drone from a single instrument hit

sources: Roads, C. — The Computer Music Tutorial (MIT Press)
Hass, J. — Introduction to Computer Music, Phase Vocoding chapter (Indiana University)
Sound on Sound — Granular Synthesis: A Practical Introduction

fields.definition: In granular synthesis, grains — very short fragments of sound, typically a few to a few hundred milliseconds long — whose emission rate or spacing is locked to the host tempo or musical clock, so grain onsets fall on note values such as 1/8 or 1/16 rather than at a free-running rate set in hertz.
fields.plain_english: Granular tools chop a sound into tiny pieces called grains. Here the grains play in time with the beat. So the little bursts land right on the groove instead of at random.
fields.purpose_function: Locking grain timing to tempo keeps granular textures rhythmically in step with the track; it exists so stuttered, chopped or clouded grain effects groove with the music instead of drifting against the beat.
fields.practical_application: A producer switches a granular sampler's grain rate or density parameter from hertz to a note division, so a stutter or grain cloud stays in time whenever the sample is triggered in the project.
common_mistakes: Assuming grain rate is always set in hertz — in a DAW it can be switched to musical note values
Setting grain size longer than the note spacing, so grains overlap and smear away the rhythm
Confusing tempo-synced grains with simple beat slicing; grains are far shorter and are re-emitted, not just cut and rearranged
scenario_contexts: Making a tempo-locked stutter or glitch fill from a vocal in a DAW
Building a rhythmic granular pad that pulses in time with a track
Designing an in-time hi-hat or texture pattern from a single sampled sound

sources: Roads, C. — The Computer Music Tutorial (MIT Press)
Sound on Sound — Granular Synthesis: A Practical Introduction

fields.definition: A sample-manipulation technique that suspends the forward progress of playback at a chosen point so the sound sustains indefinitely at that instant; it is commonly realised either by spectral (phase-vocoder) freezing of one analysis frame or by granular looping of a very short window around the freeze point.
fields.plain_english: This holds a sound still at one moment so it plays on and on. It is like pressing pause, but the sound keeps ringing. A quick sound becomes a long, steady tone.
fields.purpose_function: It turns a moment of a sound into a sustained tone or texture; it exists so technicians can hold, suspend or fill space with audio to build tension or make pads from short source material.
fields.practical_application: A technician sets a freeze point in a granular or spectral processor and engages it live or in a DAW to sustain a chord, note or ambience for as long as needed under a scene or transition.
common_mistakes: Thinking a time freeze slows the sound down — it holds one instant rather than stretching the whole timeline
Freezing on a transient or plosive, which produces an unnatural or buzzy held tone
Expecting the frozen tone to change on its own; it stays static unless you add modulation or movement
scenario_contexts: Sustaining a synth chord under a build-up in a DAW
Holding an ambience or drone live during a pause in a performance
Freezing a single word or note in sound design to stretch a dramatic moment

sources: Roads, C. — The Computer Music Tutorial (MIT Press)
Hass, J. — Introduction to Computer Music, Phase Vocoding chapter (Indiana University)
Sound on Sound — Granular Synthesis: A Practical Introduction
